name: The Drug Tax: How Pharmaceutical Distributors Sit Between Every Pill and Every Patient
deck: Three companies control 90% of U.S. drug distribution, collecting recurring spreads that have nothing to do with logistics and everything to do with structural chokehold.
core_bet: McKesson, Cencora, and Cardinal Health control ~90% of U.S. drug distribution. They sit between every manufacturer and every pharmacy, hospital, and provider. From 2023-2025, GLP-1 volume surged 100%+, creating a profit paradox: distributors gained revenue but lost margin percentage, because they are locked into percentage-of-price economics. When high-volume GLP-1 drugs flooded distribution, margins compressed. Specialty and oncology channels (McKesson's $14.2B Oncology & Multispecialty, Cencora's OneOncology) offer the escape: lower volume, higher margin per unit.

mechanism: Distribution sits as a mandatory middle layer: manufacturers produce and sell to distributors; distributors buy, hold, and sell to pharmacies and providers; patients dispense at retail. Distributors hold inventory for days or weeks. They collect a percentage spread on price (1-3%). The math is simple: $1 trillion in annual pharmaceutical flow at even 1-2% spread equals enormous absolute dollar income. But this model has a ceiling. Each pill sold reduces total pills left to distribute. Volume growth eventually flattens.

The 2023-2025 GLP-1 surge exposed this ceiling. GLP-1 volume jumped 100%+, so gross-profit dollars rose. But gross-margin percentage fell because GLP-1 drugs are high-volume commodities with thin spreads. Distributors moved more pills but earned less per pill. This is the margin paradox: more revenue, lower margin %. The response is forced: shift volume into specialty and oncology channels where unit margins are higher. McKesson's Oncology & Multispecialty reached $14.2B by Q1 FY2027. Cencora acquired OneOncology. Cardinal Health expanded service-platform monetization. These channels have lower volume but higher margin per unit and create multiple revenue streams (distribution + clinical services + data).

The chokehold is that there is no bypass. Manufacturers cannot sell direct to 60,000+ retail pharmacies and 6,000 hospitals. Distributors own the logistics network, control inventory, and have locked in exclusive or preferred relationships with most providers. This creates dependency. Manufacturers and providers must route through these three companies. There is no alternative.
why_now: Between 2023 and 2025, GLP-1 volume surged 100%+, flooding distribution with high-volume, thin-spread drugs. Distributors gained revenue but lost margin percentage. This revealed that the percentage-of-price model is structurally fragile: when volume commoditizes, spreads collapse. The margin paradox forced all three distributors to simultaneously pivot into specialty, oncology, and services. Consolidation accelerated (Cencora's OneOncology, McKesson's service expansion). The race for higher-quality spread channels is now explicit.
who_pays: Manufacturers absorb pressure on wholesale margins and face demands to guarantee channel access. Providers and hospital systems navigate increasing complexity and service-bundling costs. Patients face potential end-retail price pressure if distributors pass margin constraints downstream to pharmacies.
who_profits: Distributors profit through market concentration, switching costs, and the ability to monetize every layer: distribution spread, specialty services, data services, logistics, and financing. McKesson, Cencora, and Cardinal Health remain among healthcare's most durable businesses because they sit at the chokepoint. There is no competitor.
tension: The percentage-of-price model fractures when high-volume drugs compress spreads. Distributors cannot raise prices (competitive market). They cannot reduce costs indefinitely (logistics constraints). The pivot to specialty, oncology, and services increases operational complexity and depends on sustained pricing power in those channels. If those channels also commoditize, the margin trap closes again.
surprising_part: Despite years of industry warnings about thin margins and volume pressure, all three distributors remain extraordinarily profitable and continue to raise guidance. This is the tell. It means the structural chokehold is stronger than cost pressure. Manufacturers and providers have no choice but to use them. No matter how much margins compress in commodity distribution, the monopoly economics of the chokepoint ensure profitability.
one_sentence: Pharmaceutical distributors control the one mandatory chokepoint between every drug and every patient, collecting tolls regardless of their actual value-add.
societal_stake: Three companies control access to medicines for the entire U.S. healthcare system. Any disruption in their operations (strikes, cyber attacks, supply issues, demand shock) cascades through the entire pharmacy and hospital network. The dependence is absolute. Cost pressure from any direction (regulation, consolidation, geopolitics, drug volume shifts) can propagate through drug availability and pricing.
